title: Cadre de dix
instruction: Place des jetons dans le cadre — et regarde la place qui reste.
trayAriaOne: La barquette — il reste un jeton
saidRoom: {n} sur {cap} — encore de la place pour {left}
saidTidied: Toujours {n} sur {cap} — les jetons sont alignés, le nombre n’a pas changé
gateBody: Une bibliothèque de cadres déjà garnis — le même nombre disposé de cinq façons, les compléments à dix, des paires à comparer et les nombres de onze à dix-neuf sur les deux cadres de vingt. Gardez vos propres cadres et imprimez-les.
_notes: PANEL: native linguist + CP/CE1 teacher (cycle 2) + native B2C education-marketing writer. The English was read as a SOURCE TO AUDIT, per the brief. Four defects found — two in the English, two in the code — listed first.

=== DEFECT 1 (CODE, dead string) — AND THE SOURCE FILE ALREADY KNOWS. `routinesBtn` IS UNREACHABLE. It is declared at ten-frame.js:269 and referenced NOWHERE in the file: `grep -n 'routinesBtn' ten-frame.js` returns exactly one hit, the declaration. There is no `t('routinesBtn')`, no `labelKey:'routinesBtn'`, and `_buildBar()` (ten-frame.js:1065-1189) appends only the field chips, Aligner, Compléter, Imprimer and Mes cadres. This is the §23.6 / #39 `hintMark` defect class, in a file whose own header preaches the reachability gate. CORROBORATION, found while validating this deliverable: `_source-en.json` DOES NOT CONTAIN routinesBtn — it holds 30 keys, not the 31 the brief states — so whoever built the source already dropped it. Since apply-ten-frame-locales.js:47 takes `KEYS = Object.keys(source)`, the applier will never write that line, and ten-frame.js:269 is therefore FROZEN: a stale declaration carrying ten unreviewed locale values (fr:'Séries' among them) that no panel will ever be asked about again. ACTION: delete line 269. We have still authored 'Séries' below so the key set is complete if it is instead wired up; the applier ignores the extra key, which we verified. Note the other 'invisible' keys are NOT dead: the five field labels are reached dynamically at :1061/:1081/:1082 via `f.labelKey`, and counterLabel/showNumber/uprightLabel/orderLabel/orderRows/orderPairs are reached by the shell through `settings[].labelKey` (:311-323). Only routinesBtn is orphaned.

=== DEFECT 2 (ENGLISH, mis-sell). The paid gate advertises an affordance that is FREE. `gateBody` ends 'Keep your own frames, and print the one on screen.' But Print is deliberately NOT locked: ten-frame.js:1154-1161 states it verbatim — 'PRINT IS NOT LOCKED, and that is a deliberate break with two shipped tools… Operator-ruled' — and the handler at :1162-1169 has no entitlement check. So the Teacher-plan pitch lists, as a benefit, a button every signed-out visitor already has. In French this would read as a straightforward bait. FIX SHIPPED IN FR: we tie printing to the kept frames instead — 'Gardez vos propres cadres et imprimez-les.' Printing a frame you have SAVED genuinely is downstream of the paid feature, so the claim becomes true without removing the print mention. The English needs the same correction; we cannot make it (§21.5a and the string is not ours).

=== DEFECT 3 IS NOW FIXED AT SOURCE, AND THE FIX RETIRES OUR WORKAROUND. `trayAriaOne` was added after we reported the n=1 plural fault, and _paint() now branches three ways at :1050-1052 — empty / `left === 1` / else. THAT CHANGES THE RIGHT FRENCH FOR `trayAria`. We had written 'il en reste {n}', where the pronoun `en` carries the noun precisely BECAUSE it takes no number agreement and so survived {n}=1. With the singular split out, `trayAria` is unreachable below two, so the plural is now correct BY CONSTRUCTION and the workaround is obsolete — it was vaguer than French needs to be, and a screen-reader user heard a bare count with the counter named only by anaphora. The three forms are now parallel and each names both parts: 'La barquette — vide' / 'La barquette — il reste un jeton' / 'La barquette — il reste {n} jetons'. `trayAriaOne` deliberately carries NO placeholder: it has no entry in the applier's NEEDS table (apply-ten-frame-locales.js:36-40), so `need` is empty and ANY {token} would be rejected as stray — writing '{n}' there would halt the fan-out. NOUN CONFIRMED: all three tray strings say `la barquette`; see the tray ruling below for why it is not `le plateau`. The drift the Finnish panel flagged is NOT in this file — it is in ten-frame.js, where the hand-seeded fr `trayAriaOne` (:295) already uses 'La barquette' while :296 and :297 still hold the pre-panel 'Le plateau'; applying this panel overwrites both and the tool becomes self-consistent.

=== DEFECT 3, AS ORIGINALLY REPORTED (ENGLISH, grammar at n=1). `trayAria` 'The tray — {n} counters left' is ungrammatical at {n}=1, which is one of the most common states in the whole tool (it is reached on every board one short of full). _paint() at :1024-1026 branches only on `left > 0` vs empty, so 1 takes the plural template: 'The tray — 1 counters left'. The shipped French had the identical fault ('il reste 1 jetons'). FIX SHIPPED IN FR: 'La barquette — il en reste {n}' is grammatical at 1 and at 19 alike, because the pronoun `en` carries the noun and takes no number agreement. French can dodge this; English cannot without a second string. Flagging so EN and the other ten locales are checked — sv/da/no/nl/de all have the same singular/plural exposure.

=== DEFECT 4 (CODE, latent placeholder trap). At :1051 the substitution is asymmetric: `msg.replace('{n}', …)` and `msg.replace('{left}', …)` use STRING patterns (first occurrence only) while `{cap}` uses `/\{cap\}/g`. A locale that writes {n} or {left} twice — which several languages would want to, e.g. to repeat the count in a subordinate clause — ships a raw '{n}' into a screen reader. Undocumented and invisible until a locale trips it. Recommend making all three global. Our strings use each of {n} and {left} exactly once, so fr is safe today.

=== ALSO NOTED (CODE, a11y, lower severity). `keepsBtn` is used as the accessible name of THREE different controls: the shelf toggle chip (:1179), the '+' SAVE-THIS-BOARD button (:1295) and EVERY saved-item RESTORE button (:1309). A screen-reader user hears 'Mes cadres' for the shelf, for saving, and for each of up to twelve different restores. No string choice can repair this — three actions need three names. Not fixable by this panel; filed.

=== ALSO NOTED (CODE, reachability of saidFull). `saidFull` is announced ONLY from the Compléter handler (:1150). A child who fills the last cell BY HAND falls through to `saidBoard` (:1049-1050, because left===0) and hears '10 sur 10' rather than the full-state line. Not wrong, but the two paths to the same state announce differently. Our 'C’est plein — {cap} sur {cap}' reads correctly as the result of pressing Compléter, which is its only live caller.

=== RULING 1 — THE TRAY IS NOT `le plateau`. This was our largest change and it is a hard sibling collision. `plateau` is the exact French anatomical term for a BALANCE PAN, and number-balance owns it comprehensively: 'Mettez des nombres dans les plateaux', 'Touche le plateau le plus lourd', 'Couvrir le plateau de gauche', 'Vider les plateaux', 'Montrer ce que vaut chaque plateau', 'Remplir le plateau', plus a fractions tool's 'Le plateau — la preuve que deux quarts…'. A French teacher moving between the two tools would meet one noun naming two unrelated objects, one of which tips. REJECTED: `plateau` (owned), `le bac` (industrial, not classroom), `la réserve` (abstract — the header requires three PHYSICAL named parts, and a réserve is a quantity not an object), `la coupelle` (a science-lab dish; French primary manipulatives do not live in one). SHIPPED: `la barquette` — the plastic manipulatives tray that is on every French maternelle/CP table, physically bounded exactly as the widget draws it, and FREE across all 47 tools (zero hits). Feminine, so `vide` in trayEmptyAria agrees correctly.

=== RULING 2 — `Ranger` REJECTED for tidyBtn; SHIPPED `Aligner`. Two reasons. (a) Collision: bundle-bot-activity.js:108 already ships 'Ranger ⊞' as a control label and class-timer.js:41 owns 'Rangement' as a named classroom routine — so the bare verb is contested on the platform. (b) Precision, and this is the stronger reason: `snap()` (:441-445) sets the mask to `canonicalMask` = the FIRST n ordinals in order. That is not tidying-in-the-general-sense, it is putting them in a line from the start. `Aligner` names exactly that operation, a CP child understands it, and it keeps the announcement honest — 'les jetons sont alignés' describes what visibly happened. `Ordonner` was rejected as reading like sorting-by-value (an ordering relation), which the tool refuses (REFUSE #8). We answer the brief's question directly: the French verb for making a scattered set line up is `aligner`; `ranger` is the household 'put away' and is what the two sibling tools above use it for.

=== RULING 3 — `les compléments à dix` is CORRECT for gateBody, and it is correct BECAUSE gateBody is teacher-facing. This is the official register: 'compléments à 10' is the term in the Eduscol/programmes de cycle 2 documents a French teacher reads, and it is what she would search for. The child-facing register would be 'les amis de dix' or 'les copains de dix' — warmer, and WRONG here, because gateBody is a subscription pitch addressed to the buyer, not a prompt addressed to the class. Kept, spelled out ('dix', not '10') to sit with 'de onze à dix-neuf' in the same sentence. Note this is one of the very few strings in the tool written to an adult; the instruction and all announcements stay in the tutoiement the child hears.

=== `jetons` IS THE RIGHT WORD AND IS NOT A COLLISION — it is the house term. The brief asked whether a sibling owns it. Five tools use it (number-balance, part-whole-frame, sound-boxes, numbers-court, ten-frame-core), which sounds like a collision and is the opposite: `jeton` is the platform's settled French for a counter, exactly as Plättchen / ficha / fiche / bricka are in their locales, and no tool's IDENTITY is built on it. A CP teacher says 'des jetons'. `pion` was rejected (a pion is a game piece that MOVES ON A BOARD — it implies position matters and would fight the cardinality thesis), and `bouton` / `pastille` were rejected as not being what is in the box.

=== HEAD-TERM COLLISION WE CANNOT FIX, FLAGGED FOR THE OPERATOR. `title` is locked to 'Cadre de dix' and that is right — it is the French head term and an indexed slug. But part-whole-frame.js:88 ships the French title 'Le cadre des parts' and its instruction 'Fais passer un jeton'. So in French, and in French alone, TWO tools are 'le cadre' and both are full of jetons: de is Zehnerfeld vs 'Zahlen zerlegen', en is Ten Frame vs 'Number Bonds Board', nl is Tienraam vs 'Splitsen' — no other locale has this. The intruder is part-whole-frame, not this tool, and its title is not ours to change. Worth a look before more French copy is written around either.

=== fieldTenRow — `Dix en ligne` REJECTED, `Dix à la file` SHIPPED. Two independent problems with the shipped string. (a) `ligne` is the identity noun of TWO siblings: number-line.js:201 'Ligne numérique' and open-number-line.js:57 'La ligne des sauts'. A field chip named 'Dix en ligne' inside a third tool reads as a reference to them. (b) In contemporary French B2C copy 'en ligne' first parses as ONLINE — the exact register this tool's landing page lives in. We also rejected `rangée` (rekenrek owns it for its rods: 'Rangées par boulier', '1 rangée (jusqu’à 10)', '2 rangées (jusqu’à 20)') and `bande` (pattern-bench's strip, 'La bande le continue', plus the ruler's 'Mesure la bande'). `Dix à la file` is plain CP French, collides with nothing, and cannot be misread. NOTE THE DELIBERATE ASYMMETRY: we do use `ligne` in orderRows ('Ligne par ligne'), because there it is the table-row sense — 'une ligne d’un tableau' is the standard and unavoidable French for a grid row, and an order label is a description, not an identity.

=== uprightLabel — `Mettre debout` REJECTED for `Poser à la verticale`. `upright` swaps rows and columns (:550, :555-561); a rectangle does not 'stand up', and 'mettre le cadre debout' reads as childish where the string is in a settings drawer read by the teacher, not by the class. `à la verticale` is the precise and ordinary French. orderPairs moved from `Par paires` to `Deux par deux`: posOf under order==='pairs' (:543-545) fills a COLUMN's two cells together, and 'deux par deux' is the phrase a CP teacher actually uses at the board, where 'par paires' suggests pairing two objects with each other.

=== GENDER AND NUMBER WERE DESIGNED OUT OF THE ANNOUNCEMENTS. This is not cosmetic: `saidFull` and `saidTidied` are reused across five fields, one of which is PLURAL ('Deux cadres de dix'), so any bare past participle or predicate adjective agreeing with the field would be wrong on that field. The shipped French had exactly that fault — 'Plein, …' and '…, rangé' are masculine singular and break on 'Deux cadres'. FIX: `C’est plein` and `les jetons sont alignés` — the first takes the invariable neuter `ce`, the second agrees with `jetons` (always masculine plural), so neither depends on which field is loaded. Same reason we did not write 'Rangé :' at the head of saidTidied.

=== saidTidied CARRIES ITS INVARIANT EXPLICITLY. The code comment at :288-290 states that this string's whole job is that the number did NOT change, and that a screen-reader user has no other way to learn it. 'Toujours {n} sur {cap}' says it arithmetically; we added 'le nombre n’a pas changé' so it is also said in words, because the SR user cannot see the counters march into place — which is the entire pedagogical event the sighted class is watching (header, THE ROUTINE).

=== PICBILLE — RECOMMENDATION: LEAVE `fr` ON `default`. NO OVERRIDE NEEDED, and this is a positive finding rather than an absence of one. Brissiaud's boîtes de Picbille (J’apprends les maths) organise ten as FIVE AND FIVE in a partitioned box; the constellation a French child internalises is 5+5, not 10-in-a-line. That is `GEOM.ten` — 1 pane, 5 cols, 2 rows — exactly what `GEOMETRY_BY_LOCALE.default.single` already gives fr, and the header's own geometry correction applies verbatim in French: on a 2x5 each ROW IS FIVE and the line between the rows already IS the five-structure, so `brk:[]` is right and there is nothing to draw. So the answer to the brief's question is NO: the French tradition does not want the 1x10-with-a-break as its single frame. `tenrow` in France reads as the bande numérique / réglette, a DIFFERENT material with a different job (ordinal position), and it is correctly demoted to a third chip. For the twenty we also confirm `twentypair`: Brissiaud reaches the teens as DEUX BOÎTES (dix et encore trois), which is 'Deux cadres de dix' and is the decomposition a French CP child is taught. The German Zwanzigerfeld (`twentyfield`, one 2x10 block) has no equivalent in French practice — it is harmless as the fifth chip and a curious teacher may reach it, but it must not become the fr default. CONFIDENCE: high on `single`, high on `twenty`. Offered as a hypothesis for the operator per the file's own rule at :221-227; we changed no code.

=== TYPOGRAPHY, decided against the shipped file rather than from the rulebook. Standard French sets a narrow no-break space before ':' — but the brief forbids invisible characters, and we verified the house convention empirically: the file contains NO U+00A0 and NO U+202F anywhere, and the shipped `numeralAria` is 'Dans le cadre : {n}' with a PLAIN U+0020. We follow the house. No string needs '?', '!' or ';' — questions are forbidden by REFUSE #1 in any case — so the only French spacing rule in play is the colon, which appears once. Guillemets are not used; nothing here is quoted. The em dash U+2014 is kept as the house separator, matching every other locale in this file.

=== APOSTROPHES ARE U+2019 — ON TYPOGRAPHY, NOT ON FEAR OF BREAKAGE. 'C’est', 'n’a', 'l’offre' (three occurrences: saidTidied, saidFull, gateCta). CORRECTION TO OUR OWN FIRST DRAFT, which we verified rather than shipped: we had written that a U+0027 typewriter apostrophe would terminate the single-quoted JS literal and break ten-frame.js. THAT IS WRONG — apply-ten-frame-locales.js:83 is `esc = s => s.replace(/\\/g,'\\\\').replace(/'/g,"\\'")`, so a straight apostrophe is escaped and written safely. The real reason stands on its own: U+2019 is the correct French apostrophe, it is what the file already ships (fr 'Voir l’offre Enseignant' at :300 and every other locale), and mixing the two forms inside one string table is the kind of drift nobody reviews. A panel should not invent a breakage claim to justify a correct typographic choice.

=== gateCta contains the shipped plan name 'Enseignant' as required. gateTitle moved from 'Encore des cadres' to 'Des cadres tout prêts': 'encore' promises MORE OF THE SAME, which undersells — the paid library is not more empty frames, it is frames already set up, which is also what the body then says.

=== CHECKED AGAINST THE REFUSE LIST: no string asks a question or names an answer; none carries a verdict, a score, a comparison, an equation or a strategy step; 'Compléter' names the physical action of filling the remaining cells to the frame's own capacity, not the make-ten strategy (REFUSE #17), and it is the ordinary French for that action. 'des paires à comparer' in gateBody describes library CONTENT the teacher sets up, not an on-screen verdict (REFUSE #8). No capacity other than five, ten and twenty is named anywhere.
